title: Power sets, uncountability, and the continuum

question.text:
Which set has cardinality strictly larger than R?
(A) R × R
(B) R \ Q
(C) P(N)
(D) All finite sequences of real numbers
(E) P(R)

solution.text:
Cantor gives |P(R)| > |R|. The plane, irrationals, power set of naturals, and finite real se-
quences all have cardinality c, so they are not larger.

question.text:
If |A| = 3, how many functions A → P(A) are there?
(A) 729 (B) 512 (C) 256 (D) 24 (E) 64

solution.text:
3
The codomain has 2 = 8 elements. Each of three domain elements has eight independent
3
image choices, giving 8 = 512 functions.

question.text:
Which function is a bijection from (−1, 1) onto R?

(A) x 7→ x/(1 + x ) (B) x 7→ x/(1 − x )
2 2
(C) x 7→ x /(1 − x ) (D) x 7→ arcsin x
(E) x 7→ tan(πx)

solution.text:
2 2 2 2
The derivative of x/(1 − x ) is (1 + x )/(1 − x ) > 0, and its limits at the endpoints are
−∞ and +∞. Continuity gives surjectivity and strict increase gives injectivity. A and D
are bounded, C is not injective, and E is undefined at ±1/2.

question.text:
For a function f : A → P(A), set D = {a ∈ A : a ∈/ f (a)}. Which statement is always true?
(A) D = ∅
(B) D = A
(C) D ∈/ P(A)
(D) D ̸= f(a) for every a ∈ A
(E) D = f(a) for exactly one a ∈ A

solution.text:
If D = f(a) for some a, then a ∈ D would be equivalent to a ∈/ D, by the defining rule.
This is impossible. The set D is a subset of A, so it belongs to the codomain but is missed
by f . The proof works for every set, including the empty set.
